props.title: Flirting

sections.content: Flirting (1991) stands as one of Australian cinema's most nuanced coming-of-age stories, with director John Duigan crafting an achingly authentic portrait of first love against the backdrop of 1960s boarding school life. The film follows Noah Taylor as Danny Embling, reprising his role from The Year My Voice Broke (1987), opposite Thandiwe Newton's Thandiwe Adjewa. Their interracial romance, set against the conservative atmosphere of rural Australia during the Vietnam War era, echoes the sophisticated teen narratives of François Truffaut's The 400 Blows (1959) and Peter Weir's Dead Poets Society (1989).

sections.content: The film's treatment of adolescent relationships shares DNA with later sophisticated teen dramas like An Education (2009) and Call Me By Your Name (2017). Duigan's approach eschews typical teen movie clichés, instead focusing on intellectual awakening alongside emotional development. The philosophical discussions between Danny and Thandiwe about Sartre and existentialism elevate the material beyond conventional romance, while never losing its youthful energy and authenticity.

What sets Flirting apart is its handling of race and class in 1960s Australia, themes that would later be explored in films like Rabbit-Proof Fence (2002) and The Sapphires (2012). The film's early spotlight of Thandiwe Newton launched her career, much as Strictly Ballroom (1992) did for Baz Luhrmann in the same era of Australian New Wave cinema. sections.content: Flirting helped establish a distinctive voice in Australian coming-of-age cinema that influenced later works like Somersault (2004) and Girl Asleep (2015). The film's sensitive portrayal of teenage outsiders and its literary sensibilities created a template for intelligent youth-focused storytelling that can be seen in contemporary works like Lady Bird (2017) and Eighth Grade (2018).
